paragraphs.heading: The scales that came first
paragraphs.text: When the twentieth century began, people knew very little about how earthquakes happen, so the first magnitude scales were empirical. Richter worked out how to adjust for distance from the epicentre. With that adjustment, the logarithm of the amplitude on a seismograph trace could serve as a measure of magnitude. In 1935 he published what is now called the local magnitude scale, labelled M_L.

paragraphs.heading: The problem of saturation
paragraphs.text: The local magnitude scale was built on shallow, moderate-sized earthquakes roughly 100 to 600 km away, conditions where surface waves are predominant. When an earthquake is deeper, farther away or bigger, its surface waves are much reduced, and the scale gives too low a magnitude. This problem is called saturation. More scales were developed to overcome the deficiencies of M_L. One was Mₛ, a scale of surface-wave magnitude that Beno Gutenberg developed in 1945. All of them, though, are subject to saturation.

paragraphs.heading: Two great earthquakes
paragraphs.text: In the 1970s Mₛ was the preferred magnitude scale. It saturates around Mₛ 8.0, so it underestimates the energy released by "great" earthquakes. The Chilean earthquake of 1960 and the Alaskan earthquake of 1964 are examples. On the Mₛ scale they came out at 8.5 and 8.4, yet they were notably stronger than other earthquakes of M 8. On the moment magnitude scale they were nearer to 9.6 and 9.3.

paragraphs.heading: Modelling the source with forces
paragraphs.text: The source of an earthquake cannot be observed directly. An early step was to work out which arrangements of forces could produce seismic waves matching the ones observed from earthquakes. Take a pair of forces that are offset, acting on parallel lines that are separate. The object they act on feels a rotational force, or torque, and in mechanics this model is called a couple. Add a second couple, equal in magnitude and opposite, and the torques cancel. This is called a double couple.

paragraphs.heading: Thirty years of argument
paragraphs.text: Hiroshi Nakano showed in 1923 that a double couple model could explain certain aspects of seismic waves. This led to a controversy lasting three decades over the best model of the seismic source: a single couple or a double one. Japanese seismologists favoured the double couple, while most seismologists favoured the single couple. The debate ended with work by Maruyama (1963), Haskell (1964), and Burridge and Knopoff (1964), who modelled earthquake ruptures as dislocations. They showed that the pattern of seismic radiation can then always be matched by a pattern worked out from a double couple, and that a single couple cannot do this.

paragraphs.heading: From waves to seismic moment
paragraphs.text: These models matter in seismology because each one lets scientists derive how the waves from an earthquake should look at a distance. With that relation understood, it can be turned around: the observed seismic waves are used to determine other characteristics of the earthquake, including its fault geometry and seismic moment. Seismic moment is what the moment magnitude scale is based on. In 1966 Keiiti Aki took the 1964 Niigata earthquake and calculated its seismic moment from the seismic waves, using a double couple. The result agreed reasonably well with the seismic moment worked out from the physical dislocation that had been observed.

paragraphs.heading: How it compares with Richter
paragraphs.text: Like the local magnitude scale that Richter defined, the moment magnitude scale is logarithmic. For small earthquakes, the two scales give roughly the same magnitudes.
